07 / Writing

### How I think.

Field guide

12 min read

1.15×

rank 1 vs rank 10 under RRF at k = 60

#### RAG past the tutorial: where retrieval quietly breaks

Field guide

10 min read

1.7% vs 60%

same pass@1, very different pass^8

#### Agent orchestration, the hard parts

Field guide

8 min read

62.7 vs 99.9

same model, two harnesses, ARC-AGI-3

#### An AGI benchmark score is not a coding score

How the Decasonic platform fits together

### One database. Every app. Every agent.

01

AI Sourcing

Deal flow

One of 35+ apps. It writes signals and companies through the Hub and holds no database key.

02

AI Coach

Team guidance

Read-heavy: it pulls what it needs from the shared schema.

03

Action Portal

Briefings, actions

Reads Supabase directly with a read-only key, because analytics need joins the Hub doesn't do.

04

Investor Day

Event platform

300 attendees, live in Chicago.

05

Meeting OS

Recording to actions

10-stage pipeline: transcript to decisions, actions and follow-ups.

+30

More apps

35+ in total

Each new app is onboarded in minutes with a generated integration client.

GW

MCP Hub

Gateway · table and column permissions · logs

Every write passes here. Keys are validated, permissions enforced, errors translated.

DB

DDS v3 · Supabase

87 tables · 73 enums · 1 migration

The contract between all apps. 35 entities, 41 junction tables, 9 structural decisions.

CP

Agent Control Panel

350+ agents observed

Heartbeats, health scores, remote control, prompt versioning.

CE

Context Engine

What each agent sees

Composes right-sized, replayable context inside a token budget.

SK

Skills OS

206 agents synced

Skills are A/B tested against real agents and injected at runtime.

DS

Data Sync

CRM, Notion, transcripts

Bulk writes go direct, with an audit log, because routing them through the Hub would be 395+ round trips.

Apps write → Hub → one schema → platform services read

Hover a node for the reasoning

## Use cases

The problems I get called for, what I build for each one, and the proof that I've built it before.

Work as

Full-time · contract · studio · workshops

Core

AI products, agents & enablement

Languages

Arabic & English

Based in

[Book a 30-min call](https://cal.com/saad-altamari-y0upir/30min)

Hiring? Get my CV

01 / If this sounds familiar

### Five problems I solve.

Use case 01

#### Invisible agents

"We have agents in production and nobody can tell which ones are working, what they cost, or why one broke."

What I build

A control plane: heartbeats and health scores for every agent, cost per agent and per app, remote pause, model swap and prompt push, versioned prompts with rollback.

Proof

Agent Control Panel · 350+ agents across 35+ apps

Read the case study

Use case 02

#### Keys everywhere

"Every app holds its own database credentials, schema changes break things silently, and onboarding an app takes days."

What I build

One gateway with table- and column-level permissions, request logs, friendly errors and rate limits, plus AI-generated integration clients for each new app.

Proof

MCP Hub · onboarding went from days to minutes

Read the case study

Use case 03

#### Wrong context

"Our agents see too much, too little or the wrong thing, and we can't explain why an answer came out the way it did."

What I build

A context layer that ranks sources by value per token, keeps untrusted text out of instructions, and records every decision so it can be replayed and audited.

Proof

Context Engine · 9-stage pipeline, byte-for-byte replay

Read the case study

Use case 04

#### AI-curious team

"Our engineers want to use Claude Code, skills and MCP properly, not just paste into a chat window."

What I do

Hands-on workshops and setup sprints: Claude Code, writing skills, wiring MCP, building agents your team can trust, in Arabic or English.

Proof

190+ people across four workshops, plus five diploma cohorts

Book a workshop

Use case 05

#### An MVP that holds

"We need a product built, our budget is real but small, and we can't afford something that falls over."

What we build

With SKAI Group, the studio I co-founded: AI systems, web, mobile and SaaS. We scale the scope to your budget. Never the quality.

Proof

4 clients closed in 2 weeks · Al Delma ISO training platform

Visit SKAI Group

02 / How a project runs

### Four steps. No mystery.

Step 1 of 4

#### Map

Before I suggest anything, I measure what exists: a snapshot query of your data, a list of every app and agent, and where they actually break. Arguments start from numbers, not adjectives.

You keep

A written picture of your system, with counts

Failure classes ranked by impact

A short list of what not to touch

03 / The Claude ecosystem

### Taught by someone who ships with it.

Claude Code is my daily driver. I've built an MCP gateway, a skills CMS that A/B tests skills against real agents, and a control plane for 350+ agents.

That's the difference between a workshop that demos features and one that leaves your team with a working setup.

05 / Questions people ask

01

Do you only work with Claude?

No. My production systems run Claude, OpenAI, Gemini, Grok, Groq and OpenRouter behind one gateway with fallback chains. Claude is where I go deepest, and the toolkit I teach.

02

Can you work inside our existing stack?

Yes. My default is TypeScript, Node, PostgreSQL or Supabase and React, with Python for ML. Either way, I start by mapping what already exists before I suggest changing anything.

03

What does an audit actually look like?

A snapshot query of what's really in your database, then failure classes with counts and a fix plan for each. The last one I ran found 5 failure classes across 9 apps and took signal throughput from 78 to 864.

04

Can you show us code?

Systems I built for employers belong to them, so for those I walk you through architecture and decisions. My own projects I can show directly.

05

Arabic or English?

Both. I write, teach and present in either.

05 / How I build

### Rules that show up in everything.

01

#### Deterministic where it matters. AI where it helps.

In practice

The matcher picks pairs with pure, tested code. The LLM only writes the reason.

02

#### One gateway for every model call.

In practice

Fallback chains live in one place, and the UI says so when the primary model didn't answer.

03

#### Degrade gracefully. Never fail hard.

In practice

LLM summary, then deterministic extract, then static fallback. Compose never returns a 500.

04

#### If the database doesn't enforce it, it's a convention.

In practice

Trust tiers as CHECK constraints. Permissions at table and column level.

05

#### Let the system find it. Let a human ship it.

In practice

Improvements are proposed with evidence, approved by a person, and reverted in one click.

06

#### Argue with a query, not an adjective.

In practice

Zero cost data across 51,378 execution logs made the case faster than any slide.

07 / Beyond the browser

### Range, on purpose.

Hardware · 2026

Hemolock

A medical-device team lost their emergency-kit prototype. I rebuilt the electronics and firmware: flip one switch, and after a 5-second cancellable countdown it sends your GPS location over Telegram in Arabic and English, then places automated calls.

Countdown · cancel anytime

Research · in progress

Stroke, by microwave

Replicating a 2025 paper that detects brain hemorrhage from an antenna's reflection, without the commercial solvers it relied on. A semi-analytical model generates data, and custom FDTD solvers check the physics.

Antenna reflection, three resonances

Dashed: with a lesion · schematic

# Writing on RAG, agents and AI evaluation · Saad Tamari

URL: https://saadaltamari.com/writing

Home

/

# Context Engine · AI case study by Saad Tamari

URL: https://saadaltamari.com/case-context-engine

Home

/

Work

/

Case 03

## Context Engine

A context compiler for investment agents. It answers one question: what should this agent see, inside this budget, and why?

Role

Wrote the memo, built the engine

When

Jun–Aug 2026 · Decasonic

Stack

Node 24 · TypeScript 5.9 · Express 5

Console

React · Vite · TanStack Query

9

stages per compose

2s

hard budget, then a deterministic fallback

0

500 errors, by design

22

assertions in the verification suite

01 / The problem

### Three ways context goes wrong.

An agent asks: I'm agent X, my task is Y, it's about company Z, and I have about 6,000 tokens. What should I actually be looking at?

Most systems answer with "the top results from a vector search". That fails in three ways, and each one needed its own fix.

Too much: cost, latency and diluted signal.

Wrong: stale, cross-tenant, personal, or web text carrying an injection.

Unexplainable: nobody can say why the agent saw what it saw.

Rank by value per token, gate before ranking, and make every answer replayable.

02 / How a compose works

### Safety first. Then value.

Four ideas carry the nine stages.

Idea 01 · Gate before value

#### Reject first, with a reason.

Before anything is ranked, sources are filtered: inactive ones, human exclusions, untrusted sources for agents that can write, tenancy mismatches, personal data, workflow restrictions. Every rejection is written down with its reason.

Idea 02 · Value per token

#### Stop when the next slice isn't worth it.

Pinned sources go in first. The rest are sorted by value per token, penalized for redundancy, and packed until the marginal utility falls below a floor. Allocation stops there, even with budget left.

Idea 03 · Band the prompt

#### Untrusted text never gives orders.

The prompt is built as directive, task, evidence and a tail restatement. The lowest trust tier can never reach the directive band, enforced in code and by a database CHECK constraint. Low-trust text is wrapped as data to analyse.

Idea 04 · Learn with a human gate

#### It can find improvements. It can't ship them.

Shadow A/B runs, ablations and inclusion trials measure what each source is worth. The proposer drafts a change only with enough evidence, and a person approves it. Revert is one click.

Composed inside the 2,000 ms budget · open the trace

- Classify: the objective sorted into one of eight task types, or "general" when unsure.

- Load: the profile for this agent and task, the source catalog, measured utility and today's spend.

- Gate: rejections written down with reasons.

- Value: each source scored on task fit, entity match, trust and freshness.

- Allocate: packed by value per token until the floor.

- Assemble: fetched through the gateway, injection-scanned, tokens counted for real, near-duplicates removed.

- Band: directive, task, evidence, tail.

- Probe: an advisory check that the context is sufficient.

- Emit: a content-addressed object that replays byte for byte.

03 / The contract

### Ask once. Replay forever.

What an agent sends, and what it gets back.

Request

POST /api/dce/context/compose

{

"agent": "screener",

"objective": "Screen this inbound deck",

"entity": "company:…",

"budget_tokens": 6000

}

Response

a context object

{

"hash": "sha256:…",

"bands": ["directive", "task", "evidence", "tail"],

"slices": [ … ],

"excluded": [ { "reason": … } ],

"fallback_used": false

}

#### The judge is judged too.

An LLM scores outputs criterion by criterion, but the overall score is recomputed in code from fixed weights. The model's own total is never trusted. Rubrics are immutable: a change is a new version.

Humans label a golden set, and the system measures rank correlation, mean error and bias between its judge and the humans, so it knows how much to trust itself.

#### Six operator screens.

Compose inspector, with "replay from snapshots".

"Why this context", a printable decision record.

Frontier: quality against input tokens.

Utility, proposals and the golden set.

04 / Decisions worth explaining

01

Why stop with budget left?

Because the last few slices usually cost more attention than they add. Past the marginal-utility floor, more context dilutes the signal and raises cost and latency.

02

How does it never return a 500?

A 2-second timeout races the whole pipeline. A timeout, an exception or a rate-limit breach all return a deterministic static prompt with fallback_used set to true. Summaries degrade to deterministic extracts under 2.5 seconds, and embedding dedupe falls back to shingle overlap.

03

Where does it stop and another system start?

A clean boundary with the firm's context graph: the graph owns the directive band, meaning truth and routing. The engine owns the evidence band: fetch, budget, order and format. The graph never retrieves, and the engine never judges truth.

04

How do you know it works?

A 22-assertion verification suite runs against a live server and checks determinism, replay identity, trust-tier protection, tenancy isolation, fail-open behaviour and token accounting. The spec is executable.

Node 24

TypeScript 5.9

Express 5

Zod

Pino

gpt-tokenizer

Supabase

Claude · OpenAI · Gemini · xAI

# Agent Control Panel · AI case study by Saad Tamari

URL: https://saadaltamari.com/case-control-panel

Home

/

Work

/

Case 01

## Agent Control Panel

Mission control for 350+ agents across 35+ apps. One login, and every agent is observable, measurable and remotely controllable.

Role

Architect & builder

When

Feb–Aug 2026 · Decasonic, now SKAI Group

Stack

Express 5 · React 18 · Postgres · Drizzle

Now

A SKAI Group product · mySTARTUP

350+

agents registered

35+

apps reporting in

6

model providers, one fallback chain

~60

API endpoints on 9 tables

01 / The problem

### Hundreds of agents. Zero visibility.

The firm had agents spread across dozens of apps, each built separately. When one went quiet, nobody knew. When a prompt needed changing, someone redeployed an app. Nobody could say what an agent cost per day.

Four people needed four different things: operators wanted outages and runaway spend, prompt engineers wanted to edit without a deploy, finance wanted real token cost, and developers wanted a fast way to wire a new app in.

An agent fails silently and nobody notices for days.

Changing a prompt means redeploying the app it lives in.

There is no cost per agent, per app or per day.

The platform's own AI features are invisible too.

One control plane that fixes all four.

02 / How it works

### Four jobs. One screen.

What an operator sees, in the order they'd use it.

Step 01 · Observe

#### Every app reports in.

Registered apps push heartbeats and run reports. Each agent's status becomes running, idle, paused, stopped or error, and a rolling health score recalculates on every run. Agents can have parents, so hierarchies show up as hierarchies.

Step 02 · Control

#### Change a live agent without a deploy.

Pause, resume, stop, restart, swap the model or push a new system prompt. Each command is an HMAC-signed webhook to the live app, retried with backoff and tracked from pending to acknowledged.

Step 03 · Version

#### Prompts become assets.

Every prompt keeps its full history with one-click rollback. Feedback folds straight in with tags, and an AI reviewer scores answers from 0 to 100 with a written reason.

Step 04 · Watch itself

#### The platform is its own customer.

Its 8 internal AI features run as real tracked agents, from the integration analyzer to the error solver, so platform spend is measured with the same meters as everything else.

03 / What it feels like

### A feed you can actually read.

Every heartbeat, report and command lands in one stream. Fallbacks get an amber badge, so an operator is never told the primary model answered when it didn't.

The feed on the right is a live sketch. It is generated in your browser, not pulled from real data.

Before

the prompt lives in the app

const SYSTEM = "You are a deal screener…";

// changing this means a redeploy

const res = await openai.chat(SYSTEM, input);

// cost? errors? nobody knows

After

the Control Panel owns it

const { prompt, model } = await cp.prompt(AGENT_ID);

// GET /api/prompts/:agentId

const res = await llm(model, prompt, input);

await cp.report({ agentId, tokens, ok });

// POST /api/report → health, cost, feed

04 / Decisions worth explaining

01

Why a modular monolith, not microservices?

One Node process serves the JSON API and the compiled React app, split by module rather than by process. No broker, no worker fleet. A tool that watches moving parts should have as few of its own as possible.

02

How do you keep price discovery from costing money?

Ask a free, deterministic public price API first. Only if that fails do two AI searchers research in parallel. If they disagree, each sees the other's answer and re-checks; if they still disagree, a third model judges. Everything goes to an audit log, with per-model cooldowns and a global concurrency cap.

03

Why can't a heartbeat un-pause an agent?

Because a stopped agent has to stay stopped, even if its app keeps reporting in. Token counts are upserted atomically too, so two concurrent heartbeats can't lose a count.

04

What was the strangest production bug?

A production firewall read legitimate prompt text as an attack and blocked saves. Base64-encoding the prompt and feedback write paths got past it without weakening the firewall.

Express 5

React 18

PostgreSQL

Drizzle ORM

HMAC webhooks

OpenRouter

6 LLM providers

# Dubljly · AI case study by Saad Tamari

URL: https://saadaltamari.com/case-dubljly

Home

/

Work

/

Case 05

## Dubljly دبلجلي

Paste an English lecture. Get it back in Arabic: a synced voice-over, subtitles, a study pack, and a tutor that knows the lecture.

Role

Founder · solo build

When

2026 · live since the Amman AI Hackathon

Stack

FastAPI · React 18 · Postgres

Models

Groq · Gemini · Cerebras · Azure TTS

~25K

lines of hand-written code, plus 3,800 of tests

97

API route handlers in one FastAPI service

7

pipeline steps, run by a single worker

~30s

to the study pack, target for a 10-minute lecture

01 / The problem

### The best lectures are in English.

An Arabic-speaking student has two options: read subtitles while trying to follow the content, or wait for a human dubbing studio that will never get to that video.

Dubljly answers one question for that student: can I learn from this lecture in my own language, without waiting? It started as my graduation project and I rebuilt it from scratch for the Amman AI Hackathon.

Subtitles split attention between reading and watching.

Human dubbing costs too much for one lecture.

Arabic runs longer than English, so naive dubbing drifts off the speaker.

No way to ask a question about what was just said.

A timed Arabic voice-over, a study pack first, and a tutor for that lecture.

02 / One lecture, start to finish

### Paste a link.

A YouTube link or an upload goes into a seven-step pipeline. Here is what the student sees.

Step 01 · Fetch and transcribe

#### Get the words, with their timing.

yt-dlp fetches the video, Whisper transcribes it, and the transcript is cut into timed segments. Long work never runs inside a request: one worker thread pulls jobs from a queue table, and the student watches a six-stage progress bar.

Step 02 · Study pack first

#### Start learning in about half a minute.

The learning pack (summary, key terms and their Arabic meanings) is built before the dub, so it appears in about 30 to 40 seconds. The full dub follows in about 2 to 3 minutes. Both are spec targets, not measured figures.

Step 03 · Translate, voice, mix

#### The voice stays with the speaker.

Each segment is translated and voiced on its own, then placed at its original start time, never joined end to end. A fit ladder shortens or speeds up any clip that overruns its slot. The voice-over is mixed with the original audio and exported as MP4, with Arabic and English subtitles.

Step 04 · Ask the tutor

#### A tutor that knows the lecture.

The student can ask about what they just watched, in Arabic. The whole app is Arabic and right-to-left by default, with an English toggle, real RTL layout rules and fonts chosen for Arabic.

03 / Under the hood

### One service. No extras.

One FastAPI service serves both the API and the React app. No Redis, no Celery, no Docker. Code simplified from the real pipeline.

Adapters

no vendor SDK in the pipeline

text = stt.transcribe(audio) # Whisper today

pack = llm.run("study_pack", text) # router picks a provider

clip = tts.speak(seg.arabic, voice) # Azure or edge-tts

place(clip, at=seg.start) # never end to end

Validation

Pydantic, one retry, then fall back

out = llm.json(task, schema=StudyPack)

# invalid? retry once with the error attached

# still invalid? next provider in the router

pack = StudyPack.model_validate(out)

97 handlers: 49 GET · 38 POST · 8 PUT · 1 PATCH · 1 DELETE

24 tables

7 data-safe migrations

CI guardrails on every push

Credits, promo codes, admin console

04 / Decisions worth explaining

01

Why no Redis, Celery or Docker?

So the whole product stays one deployable service. A single background worker pulls jobs from a queue table in Postgres, and no long job ever runs inside a request handler, so the API stays responsive while lectures process.

02

Why place each clip on the timeline instead of joining them?

Arabic often runs longer than English. Joined end to end, every sentence pushes the voice further from the speaker. Placing each clip at its segment’s original start, and fitting any overrun, keeps the voice with the face.

03

What happens when a model returns broken JSON?

Structured calls ask for JSON and validate it with Pydantic. Invalid output gets one retry with the validation error attached, then the router falls back to the next provider. The stack mixes Groq, Gemini and Cerebras for language and Azure or edge-tts for voice, all swappable without touching the pipeline.

04

How does the UI stay true to the design?

The mockups are the spec. The React screens are rebuilt from them and checked against the design files with a hash check, and the frontend types mirror the documented API contract, enforced by guardrail scripts in CI.

05

What is measured, and what is a target?

The 30 to 40 second study pack and the 2 to 3 minute dub for a 10-minute lecture are spec targets, not measured figures. There are no user or revenue numbers yet, so none are claimed here.

Python 3.12

FastAPI

SQLModel

Alembic

Pydantic

Groq Whisper

Gemini

Cerebras

Azure Speech

yt-dlp

ffmpeg

React 18

Tailwind 4

TanStack Query

Clerk

Postgres

# Flora AI · AI case study by Saad Tamari

URL: https://saadaltamari.com/case-flora

Home

Case 08

## Flora AI

An Arabic AI nutritionist that builds meal plans from your profile, and the first startup I founded.

Role

Founder & AI developer

When

Jan 2024 – Jan 2025 · Jordan

Stack

Python · LangChain · LangGraph · RAG

Backed by

Incubated by INJAZ

100+

leads in 3 days

$0

spent on ads

1.7K+

video views

1.1K+

landing-page visitors

01 / The problem

### Generic advice, in the wrong language.

Most nutrition apps give the same plan to everyone, and few are built for Arabic speakers. Personal guidance from a nutritionist exists, but it costs money and time most people won’t spend.

And an AI that invents a meal plan is worse than no plan at all. Accuracy had to come before fluency.

02 / How it works

### Grounded plans that follow up.

Profile

goals, body, habits

Retrieve

nutrition knowledge

Plan

grounded, specific meals

Check in

adaptive follow-ups

Track

assessment and visuals

03 / Decisions worth explaining

### Why it’s built this way.

01

#### Retrieval over raw generation

Meal plans are built on retrieved nutrition knowledge, not generated from the model’s memory, because a hallucinated meal plan is worse than none.

02

#### Prompts tuned for specifics

The prompt system was tuned for nutritionally accurate, specific output: quantities and real foods, not vague advice.

03

#### Follow up, don’t answer once

Adaptive check-ins ask how the plan is going and adjust, instead of ending the conversation after one answer.

04

#### Launch with content, not ads

Every lead came from organic video content. It proved people wanted it before any money went into marketing.

04 / What came out of it

### Proof that people wanted it.

- 1.7K+ video views, 1.1K+ landing-page visitors and 100+ leads in three days, with no ad budget.

- 3rd place in Jordan at IEEE NETC, qualifying for the Region 8 semi-finals.

- Top 7 at the Jordan Entrepreneurship Competition, and incubation with INJAZ.

- The lesson I still use: validate demand with real people before scaling the build.

# Hemolock · AI case study by Saad Tamari

Case 11

## Hemolock

An emergency kit for a medical-device team. Flip one switch, and it sends your GPS location and places a phone call.

Role

Rebuilt the electronics & firmware

When

2026

Stack

ESP32 · NEO-6M GPS · Twilio

Status

Working prototype

1

switch to trigger

5s

cancellable countdown

2

languages in every alert

3.7→5V

stable power from a LiPo

01 / The problem

### A lost prototype and a deadline.

A medical-device team lost their emergency-kit prototype and needed it working again. The idea was simple: in an emergency, one action should tell the right people where you are.

The hard parts were all physical: unstable power, firmware crashes and the real-world rules for placing automated calls in Jordan.

02 / How it works

### One switch, three things happen.

Switch

flip to arm

Countdown

5 seconds, cancellable

Locate

GPS fix

Alert

Telegram, Arabic and English

Call

automated via Twilio

03 / Decisions worth explaining

### Why it’s built this way.

01

#### A countdown you can cancel

An LED and buzzer start a 5-second countdown, so an accidental flip never sends a false alarm.

02

#### Bilingual by default

Every alert goes out in Arabic and English, with a Google Maps link to the exact location.

03

#### Stable power first

A 3.7V LiPo boosted to a stable 5V, because GPS and WiFi fail in strange ways on a sagging supply.

04

#### No blocking code

Watchdog crashes came from blocking buzzer tones. Rewriting them as non-blocking fixed the resets.

04 / What made it work

### Hardware is honest.

- A working kit: switch, countdown, GPS fix, bilingual Telegram alert and automated calls.

- Power and watchdog issues found and fixed at the root, not worked around.

- Jordan’s high-risk call permissions handled, so automated calls actually connect.

- Proof that I can take a system from firmware to the phone in someone’s pocket.

# Investor Day App · AI case study by Saad Tamari

URL: https://saadaltamari.com/case-investor-day

Home

/

Work

/

Case 04

## Investor Day App

An invite-only networking engine for 300 founders, VCs and LPs at Willis Tower, Chicago. One question per person: who should I talk to right now?

Role

Architect & builder

When

Apr–Jul 2026 · Decasonic

Stack

Expo · React 19 · Express 5 · Postgres

Shipped as

iOS, Android, PWA + admin

300

attendees, live, in one day

~60K

lines of hand-written TypeScript

124

API operations from one OpenAPI spec

188

unit tests on the parts that decide

01 / The problem

### Not a conference app. A room-reader.

About 300 people, eight hours, and a theme: investing in adoption. Every attendee wants the same thing from a day like that: the handful of people in the room worth meeting, and something to say when they get there.

The agenda alone was 21 sessions and 47 speakers, but the hard part wasn't the agenda. It was being fair to everyone, protecting the people who asked to stay private, and moving real people around a lunch hall on time.

An LLM picking matches is untestable and unfair.

Big funds crowd out everyone else.

Private attendees leak through generated text.

Imports the night before break printed QR codes.

Deterministic matching, privacy in the architecture, imports you can trust.

02 / How the day runs

### Match. Explain. Move. Protect.

The four systems that ran the room.

Step 01 · Match

#### Pure code decides who meets.

scorePair is a pure, tested function with no LLM in it. On top sit fairness rules: colleagues never match, small boosts for people with no matches yet, caps per company, and a floor so nobody ends with zero.

Step 02 · Explain

#### Emma tells you why.

The AI concierge gets a context assembled per request: the people most relevant to you, the speakers, the live agenda and the venue. Claude answers, with OpenAI as fallback through one gateway.

Step 03 · Move

#### Software that moves people.

Nine portfolio companies at numbered tables, nine timed rounds, and every attendee routed so they meet every company. A draft, published, locked state machine keeps a live rotation from being corrupted mid-lunch.

Step 04 · Protect

#### Privacy in the architecture.

Hidden attendees are masked on the server, on every surface, including inside LLM prompts. Emails never enter a prompt. Responses are shaped so that "not published" and "not grouped" look identical.

03 / The tempting version

### Why the LLM doesn't match.

Left: what most people would ship. Right: what ran in Chicago.

Tempting

ask the model to pick

const picks = await llm(

`Here are 300 attendees. Who should ${me} meet?`

);

// untestable, unfair, and private people

// are now inside a prompt

Shipped

code decides, the model explains

function scorePair(a, b) {

if (sameCompany(a, b)) return -Infinity;

let s = fit(a, b) + fit(b, a);

s += fairness(b); // +8 at zero, −4 at 10+

return s;

}

// caps, a starvation floor, then one line of "why"

04 / Decisions worth explaining

01

How do you import data the night before without breaking anything?

Upload a spreadsheet, stage the rows, let the server recompute the diff, preview it, then publish in one transaction guarded by a staged-status check. Two admins publishing at once get a 409. Session IDs survive re-imports, so printed QR codes never break, and ambiguous rows go to a human.

02

What stops someone scanning a QR and pretending to be you?

A QR code only names a target. Who you are always comes from your session token. Check-ins are idempotent, so scanning twice can't double-count.

03

Why is it invite-only?

Attendee records are created on the first authenticated request, only for invited people. Signing up on your own grants nothing.

04

What happens on a fresh production database?

It boots lunch-ready. Startup reconcilers seed the invitation template, the nine rounds and nine tables, idempotently, without overwriting anything an admin changed. One switch, event mode, moves the whole app through before, live and after.

# JoFotara POS · AI case study by Saad Tamari

URL: https://saadaltamari.com/case-jo-fotara

Home

/

Work

/

Case 09

## JoFotara POS

A multi-tenant point of sale built to Jordan’s UBL 2.1 e-invoicing standard, with zero third-party packages.

Role

Solo builder

Where

Jordan

Stack

Node.js · SQLite · UBL 2.1

Model

Setup fee + monthly per branch

0

npm dependencies

UBL 2.1

government e-invoice schema

13

automated tests

2

delivery channels: WhatsApp and SMS

01 / The problem

### Tax documents can’t depend on luck.

Jordan’s e-invoicing system requires every invoice in a strict XML format, submitted to a government platform. Small shops need that without hiring a developer.

Software that produces tax documents also carries a quieter risk: every third-party package is a dependency that can break, change or be compromised years later.

02 / How it works

### From sale to submitted invoice.

Sale

at the counter

UBL 2.1 XML

hand-built, validated

Submit

with an idempotency key

Deliver

WhatsApp or SMS

Analyse

AI insights for owners

03 / Decisions worth explaining

### Why it’s built this way.

01

#### Zero dependencies

XML namespaces, the HTTP client, encoding and validation are all hand-built to the government schema. No supply-chain surface, no dependency drift, and it still builds years from now.

02

#### Idempotent submission

A retry can never submit the same invoice twice. A double-submitted invoice is a compliance problem, not just a bug.

03

#### Multi-tenant from day one

Branches and businesses share one system with clean separation, which is what makes per-branch pricing possible.

04

#### Insights, not just records

An admin layer turns raw transactions into answers for owners on demand, using AI analytics.

04 / What it proves

### Compliance without a single package.

- A complete point of sale that speaks the government’s invoice format natively.

- A 13-test suite around the parts that matter most: XML generation, validation and retry.

- A business model built in: a setup fee plus a monthly fee per branch.

- A constraint that became the feature: nothing to audit, nothing to update, nothing to break.

# MCP Hub · AI case study by Saad Tamari

URL: https://saadaltamari.com/case-mcp-hub

Home

/

Work

/

Case 02

## MCP Hub

An air-traffic controller for data. Every app talks to the Hub, the Hub talks to the database, and no app holds a credential.

Role

Architect & builder

When

Feb–Aug 2026 · Decasonic

Stack

Next.js 14 · Supabase · SSE

Models

Anthropic → OpenAI → xAI

35+

codebases that no longer hold DB keys

87

tables behind one gateway

11×

signal throughput after the audit

Min

to onboard an app, down from days

01 / The problem

### Every app had the keys to everything.

Before the Hub, database credentials sat in 35+ codebases. There was no central visibility, no least privilege, and a schema change could break an app without anyone hearing about it. Onboarding a new app was a manual, multi-day job.

I had already designed the shared 87-table schema. The Hub is what made it safe to share.

Credentials copied into every codebase.

No record of who wrote what, or when.

Schema changes break apps silently.

New integrations take days by hand.

One gateway, strict per-app rules, and generated clients.

02 / One request, start to finish

### Follow a single write.

POST /api/gateway with an API key and a payload. Here is what happens to it.

Step 01 · Authenticate

#### Who is asking?

The key is validated and the app's status checked. Apps move from pending to configured to active, and promote themselves on their first successful request.

Step 02 · Authorize

#### What are they allowed to touch?

Rate limits and timeouts first, then permissions at the level of the table and the column. An app can be allowed to read a table and still be blocked from one field in it.

Step 03 · Execute and log

#### Do it, and write it down.

The query runs against Supabase, the request is logged with sensitive values stripped, and raw database errors come back as friendly 400 and 409 messages.

Step 04 · Onboard the next app

#### An AI handshake between apps.

Paste a new app's discovery file. The model recommends permissions, you review them, and the Hub generates a complete integration client in JS, TS or Python, plus a prompt to paste back into the app's builder.

03 / Before and after

### Drag the line.

A database health audit across the connected apps. Left: what I found. Right: after the fixes.

Before the audit

Signals flowing

78

Signals linked to their source run

0

Agent runs recorded

0

Apps fixed

0

~400 CHECK failures from 'prod' vs 'PROD'. Zero rows in every junction table. '[object Object]' saved as a UUID.

After the fixes

Signals flowing

864

Signals linked to their source run

777

Agent runs recorded

72

Apps fixed

9

Five failure classes, a four-section fix-prompt template, and permission gaps closed in four apps.

Two lessons I carry everywhere: a gateway 200 doesn't mean the data is useful, and regressions happen during redeploys.

Before

every app holds every key

const db = createClient(URL, SERVICE_ROLE_KEY);

await db.from('signals').insert(row);

// no permissions, no log, no warning

After

one gateway, least privilege

await fetch(HUB + '/api/gateway', {

method: 'POST',

headers: { 'x-api-key': process.env.HUB_KEY },

body: JSON.stringify({ operation: 'insert', table: 'signals', data: row })

});

// checked, rate limited, permitted, logged

04 / Decisions worth explaining

01

When do you go around your own gateway?

Twice, on purpose. Bulk sync writes directly: without upsert, a 150-record sync would take 395+ round trips and hit the rate limit, so it writes straight to the database and still logs to the audit table. Analytics reads go direct with a read-only key, because a dashboard needs joins and window functions the gateway doesn't do.

02

What did the first integration teach you?

It hit foreign-key violations, because the generator wasn't passing relationship information into the prompt. I fixed it in the generator, once, and every later integration inherited the fix.

03

Why write meanings into the schema?

Human-written table and column descriptions feed the code generator. That's the difference between knowing a status column is a varchar and knowing it's a deal pipeline stage.

04

What if a model fails halfway through generating a client?

Generation streams over server-sent events with automatic fallback from Anthropic to OpenAI to xAI if a provider fails or truncates.

Next.js 14

Supabase Auth

PostgreSQL

Server-sent events

Schema introspection

3 LLM providers

## AI Product Enhancer

# Agent Skills OS · AI case study by Saad Tamari

URL: https://saadaltamari.com/case-skills-os

Home

/

Work

/

Case 06

## Agent Skills OS

A content system and test lab for the skills AI agents load at runtime. Skills are A/B tested against real agents, and the losers get rewritten.

Role

Architect & builder

When

May–Aug 2026 · Decasonic

Stack

TypeScript · OpenRouter · Zod

Status

Live

206

live agents synced

6

steps in the skill loop

2

runs per test, with and without

0

agents broken when it goes down

01 / The problem

### Skills written once, and never tested.

A skill is a block of instructions an agent loads at runtime. Most teams write one, paste it into a prompt and hope it helps. Nobody can say whether a given skill made a given agent better or worse.

With hundreds of agents in production, that guesswork compounds. A bad skill quietly degrades every agent it is assigned to, and nothing flags it.

02 / How it works

### Write, test, judge, improve.

Create

write, upload or generate a SKILL.md

Version

every save is an immutable snapshot

A/B test

same prompt, real agent, twice

Judge

structured verdict

Improve

losers rewritten

Deploy

assign and pin per agent

03 / Decisions worth explaining

### Why it’s built this way.

01

#### Test on the real agent

The lab runs the same prompt through a synced production agent twice, once with its normal system prompt and once with the skill, on that agent’s own model. No simulations.

02

#### Let the loser be rewritten

If a skill loses, a frontier model rewrites it into a new version from both outputs and the judge’s reasoning. Then it gets tested again.

03

#### Fail open

Agents pull skills at prompt-fetch time. If the service is down they fall back to their base prompts instead of breaking. An outage here must never take down the fleet.

04

#### Filter what the model suggests

A suggestions engine proposes new skills from real usage. Any agent or skill ID it hallucinates is dropped by schema validation before it reaches the screen.

04 / What I learned

### The integration was the hard part.

- Wiring it into the Agent Control Panel took three debugging rounds: two path mismatches, then auth, solved with a dedicated inbound key instead of a fake app row that would have polluted the dashboard.

- A 5-minute cache on the control-plane side means skill changes need a cache clear after reassignment. Documented, not hidden.

- My own audit caught a real bug: pinned versions should have overridden the “ready” filter, and didn’t.

- 206 agents synced and pulling skills in production.

Need something like this? I build these end to end, as a full-time engineer, on contract, or with SKAI Group.

# Agent orchestration, the hard parts · Saad Tamari

URL: https://saadaltamari.com/writing-agent-orchestration

Home

/

Writing

/

Field guide

## Agent orchestration, the hard parts

The loop is ten lines. Everything that makes it survive real traffic lives around it: reliability you can measure, side effects that happen once, a context that stays cheap, and tool output you never trust.

Saad Al-Tamari

Field guide · Agent orchestration

10 min read

Agents

Orchestration

Reliability

Security

An agent framework gives you a loop. Production gives you everything the loop ignores: runs that succeed once and fail the next time, side effects that happen twice, contexts that grow until they cost more than the answer, and tool output that turns into instructions. This note is about those parts.

### Measure reliability as pass^k, not pass@1

Benchmarks usually report pass@1, or pass@k, where a task counts as solved if any of k attempts succeeds [1]. Users don’t experience pass@k. They experience the same agent on the same kind of task, again and again. τ-bench made this explicit with pass^k, the probability that all k trials of a task succeed. In its retail domain, state-of-the-art function-calling agents such as GPT-4o solved fewer than half the tasks, and pass^8 fell below 25% [2].

pass@k = 1 − C(n − c, k) / C(n, k) pass^k = C(c, k) / C(n, k)

Unbiased estimators from n trials of a task with c successes, averaged over tasks

The non-obvious part: pass^k depends on how failures are distributed across tasks, not only on the average.

- System A | System B

- How it fails | Every task succeeds 60% of the time | 60% of tasks always pass, 40% always fail

- pass@1 | 60% | 60%

- pass^8 | 1.7% | 60%

Computed exactly. The same pass@1, and a 36× difference in pass^8. Reliability lives in the variance, not the mean

System A looks fine on a leaderboard and is unusable in a workflow, because no task is dependable. System B is honest about what it can’t do, and you can route around it. When you improve an agent, check whether pass^k moved, not only pass@1. METR’s time-horizon work makes the same point from another angle: the length of task frontier agents complete at 50% success has doubled roughly every seven months since 2019, and the horizon at higher reliability thresholds is much shorter [3]. “Can do” and “reliably does” are different curves.

p = 0.95

p = 0.80

p = 0.60

x-axis: k, number of trials that must all pass

pass^k when every task has the same per-trial success p. Real systems sit between this curve and System B

### Plan as a graph, execute in parallel

ReAct interleaves reasoning and tool calls in one loop [4]. It is flexible and pays for it: every observation goes back through the model, and every step waits for the one before. ReWOO separates planning from observation: a planner writes the whole plan with placeholders, workers fill them, and a solver composes the answer, which cuts token use substantially [5]. LLMCompiler compiles the plan into a dependency graph of function calls and runs them in parallel as soon as their inputs are ready [6].

ReAct loop

think

tool A

think

tool B

think

tool C

answer

Planned DAG

plan

A ∥ B

C

answer

start

time →

Same three tools. Independent calls run together once the plan exists

Planning up front has a second benefit that matters more than speed. If the plan is fixed before any untrusted data is read, a malicious tool result can’t add steps to it. Plan-then-execute is one of the core patterns in the prompt-injection design work below [7]. Re-planning is still allowed, but it becomes an explicit, logged transition rather than something a web page can trigger.

### Treat the context window as a cache

For long-running agents the prompt is mostly input. Manus reported about 100 input tokens per output token and called KV-cache hit rate the single most important metric for a production agent; with Claude Sonnet at the time, cached input cost $0.30 per million tokens against $3 uncached [8]. Cache hits need byte-identical prefixes, which turns some innocent habits into expensive bugs.

Breaks the cache

A timestamp at the top of the system prompt. Tools added or removed mid-run. JSON serialised with unstable key order. Rewriting earlier turns to tidy the history.

Keeps the cache

A stable system prompt and tool list. Append-only history. Deterministic serialisation. Tools masked at decode time instead of removed.

Prompt-layout choices that decide whether you pay for the prefix once or on every step

Three more Manus lessons are worth stealing. Use the file system as unbounded, restorable memory: drop a page’s content from context but keep its URL or path. Leave failed actions and stack traces in context, because erasing them removes the evidence the model needs to avoid repeating the mistake. And have the agent rewrite its task list near the end of the context, which keeps the global goal where models attend most reliably [8, 9].

### Temperature zero is not reproducibility

The usual explanation for nondeterminism at temperature 0 is floating-point arithmetic under concurrency. Thinking Machines showed the bigger cause in inference servers is a lack of batch invariance: kernels return slightly different numbers depending on batch size, and batch size depends on whoever else is using the server at that moment [10].

1,000

completions at temperature 0

80

distinct outputs

103

first token where runs diverged

1

distinct output with batch-invariant kernels

Qwen3-235B, one prompt, as reported by Thinking Machines

Two consequences for agents. Replay has to use recorded model outputs and tool results, not re-execution, or the debugger will show you a different run. And every eval needs repeated trials per task, which is pass^k again.

### Constrain the interface, not the thinking

Constrained decoding guarantees syntactically valid output by masking tokens that would break a grammar or schema [11]. It fixes parsing, not correctness, and it has a cost: Tam et al. found a significant decline in reasoning under strict format restrictions [12]. Two patterns keep both properties. Let the model reason in free text and emit the structured result in a second, constrained step. Or put a free-text reasoning field before the answer fields in the schema, so generation order follows thought order. Then validate semantically (the ID exists, the amount is in range) and return failures to the model as tool results; one retry with the error attached fixes a large share of bad calls.

### Side effects need idempotency or compensation

Retries are the right response to transient failure and dangerous around side effects. The classic answer is idempotency: key each operation so that doing it again returns the first result [13]. Derive the key from the run and the step, and store the result before acknowledging.

One side-effecting step

sketch

key = f"{run.id}:{step.id}"

if (done := ledger.get(key)): return done # a retry replays, never redoes

args = schema.validate(call.args) # reject bad arguments early

result = tool.run(args, idempotency_key=key)

ledger.put(key, result) # checkpoint before moving on

Some actions can’t be made idempotent, and some multi-step tasks have to be undone halfway. Databases solved this decades ago with sagas: split a long transaction into steps, give each step a compensating action, and on failure run the compensations in reverse [14]. For agents the rule becomes: every tool with a side effect declares either an idempotency key or a compensation, and the planner schedules irreversible steps, such as sending a message or charging a card, as late as possible, after everything that can fail has already succeeded.

Reserve slot

undo: release it

Draft invoice

undo: void it

Charge card

the pivot: irreversible

Send confirmation

retry with a key

A saga for an agent workflow. Everything before the pivot can be undone; everything after it must be safely retryable

### Multi-agent: spend tokens on breadth, keep one writer

Anthropic’s research system, a lead agent delegating to parallel subagents, beat a single agent by 90.2% on their internal research eval. It also used about 15 times the tokens of a chat interaction, and on BrowseComp, token usage alone explained 80% of the variance in performance [15]. Cognition argued the other side in “Don’t Build Multi-Agents”: subagents that can’t see each other’s context make conflicting implicit decisions, so context should be shared in full and actions kept single-threaded [16].

The two positions are consistent once you separate reading from writing. Research is breadth-first reading: independent subtasks, results merged by a lead, no conflicting side effects. Coding and operations are writing: every action carries decisions the next one depends on. Fan out to read; keep a single writer for decisions and side effects.

System design

Disobeying the spec, repeating steps

Failures baked into roles, prompts and stop conditions.

Inter-agent misalignment

Withholding, ignoring, derailing

Agents that don’t share what they know, or ignore what others said.

Task verification

Stopping early, checking badly

No verification, or verification that passes wrong work.

The three categories of MAST, a taxonomy of 14 failure modes built from 1,600+ traces across 7 frameworks, with inter-annotator agreement of κ = 0.88

That taxonomy comes from Cemri et al. [17]. The uncomfortable finding is how many failures are organisational, not model errors: unclear roles, missing verification, information one agent had and never passed on.

### Security: break the lethal trifecta

Simon Willison’s framing is the most useful threat model I know for agents: an agent that has access to private data, is exposed to untrusted content, and can communicate externally can be tricked into exfiltrating that data [18]. Remove any one of the three and that class of attack closes.

01

Private data

Mail, files, databases, credentials the agent can read.

02

Untrusted content

Web pages, inbound email, documents, tool output.

03

A way out

Sending messages, making requests, rendering links or images.

Any agent holding all three at once is one injected instruction away from a leak

When you can’t remove one, design for it. AgentDojo benchmarks agents against realistic injection attacks [19]. CaMeL separates a privileged model that plans from a quarantined model that parses untrusted data, while an interpreter tracks where every value came from and enforces which values may flow into which tools [20]. Beurer-Kellner et al. catalogue patterns with provable properties: action selectors, plan-then-execute, map-reduce over untrusted inputs, dual LLMs, code-then-execute and context minimisation [7]. Each trades flexibility for a guarantee, which is the right trade wherever money, data or reputation is involved.

### Workflows first, still

Anthropic’s guide draws the line between workflows, where code decides the path, and agents, where the model does, and recommends the simplest option that works [21]. Everything above is the cost of moving right on that spectrum.

Single call

one prompt

Chain

fixed steps

Router

model picks a branch

Orchestrator + workers

model splits the work

Autonomous agent

model owns the loop

Left to right: more flexibility, less predictability, more cost

An agent is a distributed system with a probabilistic component. Engineer it like one: measure pass^k, protect the cache, key every side effect, and assume tool output is hostile.

### References

# An AGI benchmark score is not a coding score · Saad Tamari

URL: https://saadaltamari.com/writing-agi-benchmarks

Home

/

Writing

/

Field guide

## An AGI benchmark score is not a coding score

GPT-6 Astra hit 99.9% on ARC-AGI-3 and gained about two points on the coding indexes. Here is why both are true, and what it says about reading any benchmark.

Saad Al-Tamari

Field guide · AGI benchmarks and coding

8 min read

Benchmarks

ARC-AGI

Evaluation

Coding agents

In September, GPT-6 Astra posted 99.9% on ARC-AGI-3, the benchmark designed to measure general intelligence. In the same launch, its numbers on the coding agent indexes moved by about two points. Both facts are true. The gap between them is the most useful thing to understand about benchmarks right now.

### What ARC is trying to measure

ARC starts from François Chollet’s definition of intelligence as skill-acquisition efficiency: how quickly a system learns new tasks relative to its priors and experience, not how much it already knows [1]. ARC-AGI-1 tested that with small grid puzzles, each a new rule to infer from a few examples. It held for five years, until a preview of OpenAI’s o3 scored 75.7% on the semi-private set at $26 per task, and 87.5% with about 172 times the compute, at $4,560 per task [2].

ARC-AGI-2 raised the difficulty and calibrated its tasks against a human panel [3]. ARC-AGI-3, launched on 25 March 2026, changed the format entirely: hundreds of turn-based game environments with no instructions, no rules and no stated goals. An agent has to explore, work out how the world behaves, discover what winning means, and carry that knowledge into harder levels. At launch, humans solved 100% of the environments and frontier AI scored 0.51% [4]. Scoring rewards action efficiency against a human baseline: for each level, the median action count of the roughly 500 members of the public who completed it [5].

### Six months from 0.51%

25 Mar · frontier AI at launch

0.51%

24 Jul · Claude Opus 5, high effort

30.2%

3 Sep · GPT-6 Astra, standard harness, max

62.7%

3 Sep · GPT-6 Astra, provider adapter, high

99.9%

ARC-AGI-3 results verified by ARC Prize

Those are ARC Prize’s verified results [6, 7]. On ARC-AGI-2 the frontier is now in the 90s: ARC Prize lists Claude Opus 5 at 90.4% and GPT-6 Astra at 95.0% at maximum reasoning effort. ARC-AGI-2 launched in March 2025. It took about eighteen months to get from hard to nearly saturated.

### The harness is part of the score

The same model at the same maximum effort scored 62.7% under ARC Prize’s standard harness and 98.6% under OpenAI’s provider-adapter harness [5].

- Reasoning effort | Standard | Cost | Provider adapter | Cost

- Max | 62.7% | $26,098 | 98.6% | $17,332

- XHigh | 59.3% | $37,317 | 98.4% | $18,147

- High | 54.8% | $40,705 | 99.9% | $18,817

- Medium | 38.6% | $48,090 | 98.4% | $19,285

- Low | 17.5% | $38,166 | 98.0% | $21,298

- None | 35.2% | $49,791 | 96.7% | $23,457

GPT-6 Astra on ARC-AGI-3 by harness and effort, as verified by ARC Prize. Costs are totals for the run

The difference is memory. The standard harness is provider-neutral and lets the model carry forward notes it chooses to keep. The provider adapter preserves the model’s opaque reasoning state between requests and compacts long conversations. On the 167 game runs both harnesses solved, the adapter was about 3.66 times faster and used 49% fewer tokens. OpenAI’s footnote says its harness changes two settings to better match real-world performance and does not target ARC-AGI-3 specifically [8].

Three details in that table are easy to miss. Under the standard harness, no reasoning (35.2%) beat low reasoning (17.5%): effort is not monotonic once the model has to manage its own memory. The adapter runs were cheaper as well as better, because carrying state forward avoids re-deriving it every turn. And the 36-point gap between harnesses is larger than the gap between Claude Opus 5 and Astra on the standard harness (30.2% against 62.7%). A score belongs to a model, a harness, an effort setting and a budget, together.

ARC Prize’s own position is careful. It reports both harnesses, says it believes a future AGI should be able to solve ARC-AGI-3 under the standard conditions, and states that saturating the benchmark would not be proof of AGI [5].

### Why the reasoning jump didn’t show up in coding

ARC-AGI-3

+82.1 pts

Terminal-Bench 4.0

+20.6

Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index v1.4

+1.9

DeepSWE v1.1

+1.4

Gains from GPT-5.6 Sol to GPT-6 Astra, taken from OpenAI’s own launch table

Those deltas come from OpenAI’s launch table [8]. Independently, Artificial Analysis placed Astra at 67 on its Coding Agent Index when run through Codex: roughly level with Claude Opus 5 and Fable 5, and three points behind Claude Fable 5.1 in Claude Code at 70 [9]. At launch, the coding picture was a tie at the top, not a leap.

That is not a contradiction. ARC-AGI-3 rewards inducing the rules of a small, novel world from scratch, with little state and few actions. Everyday software engineering rewards nearly the opposite: navigating a large existing codebase, following conventions nobody wrote down, keeping long chains of edits consistent, and knowing when a change is actually done. The bottleneck there is context management and engineering judgment inside a huge, specific world, not abstraction from nothing. The largest coding-adjacent gain in OpenAI’s table, Terminal-Bench, is also the task closest to ARC’s interactive explore-and-act format. That last point is my reading of the numbers, not a claim either lab makes.

### Coding benchmarks have their own problems

The coding side is not a clean yardstick either. SWE-bench turned real GitHub issues into tasks [10], and its human-validated Verified subset became the standard score. In February 2026 OpenAI stopped reporting it: auditing 138 problems that o3 did not solve consistently, it found 59.4% had material problems in their tests or descriptions, and every frontier model it tested could reproduce gold patches or verbatim problem details for some tasks [11]. Earlier, Liang et al. showed models could identify the buggy file from the issue text alone up to 76% of the time on SWE-bench repositories, against up to 53% on repositories outside it, a gap consistent with memorisation [12].

Buggy file named from issue text alone: SWE-bench repos

up to 76%

The same test on repos outside SWE-bench

up to 53%

Audited Verified problems with flawed tests or descriptions

59.4%

Two independent signs that a famous coding benchmark stopped measuring what it claimed

Benchmarks can also disagree with people. In METR’s randomised controlled trial, 16 experienced open-source developers took 19% longer on 246 real tasks when allowed to use early-2025 AI tools, after forecasting a 24% speedup and while estimating afterwards that they had been 20% faster [13]. The tools have improved a lot since, so the number shouldn’t be generalised. The method should: self-reported productivity is not a measurement.

Leaderboards built on human votes have their own version of this. The Leaderboard Illusion documented 27 private variants tested by Meta ahead of the Llama 4 release, and estimated that Google and OpenAI received about 19.2% and 20.4% of all arena data, against 29.7% for 83 open-weight models combined [14]. Contamination-resistant designs exist: LiveCodeBench only scores problems published after a model’s training cutoff [15].

### How I read a benchmark claim now

- Which set? Public, semi-private or private. Public sets leak into training data.

- Who ran it? Vendor-reported or independently verified, and under which harness and effort setting.

- What did it cost? Cost per task changes the meaning of a score. 87.5% at $4,560 a task is a research result, not a product.

- How many attempts? pass@1, pass@k or best-of-n, and whether the intervals overlap.

- Saturated or contaminated? Near-ceiling scores and pre-cutoff public data both shrink what a benchmark can tell you.

- Does it look like my work? If not, build a small private eval from my own repositories and tickets, and trust it over any leaderboard.

A benchmark measures a model, a harness and a budget on one kind of task. The skill is reading which of those actually moved.

# Dubbing Arabic without drifting off the speaker · Saad Tamari

URL: https://saadaltamari.com/writing-arabic-dubbing

Home

/

Writing

/

Build note

## Dubbing Arabic without drifting off the speaker

The obvious way to dub a lecture is to translate it, voice it and join the clips. In Arabic, that slowly pulls the voice away from the face.

Saad Al-Tamari

From the work: Dubljly · 2026

2 min read

Arabic AI

Speech

Product

Dubljly turns an English lecture, from a YouTube link or an upload, into Arabic: a synced voice-over, Arabic and English subtitles, a study pack, and a tutor that knows the lecture. I built it solo, as one FastAPI service with a React front end and no extra infrastructure.

Fetch

yt-dlp

Transcribe

Whisper

Segment

timed chunks

Study pack

shown first

Translate

Arabic

Voice

one clip per segment

Mix

over the original

The seven-step pipeline, run by a single background worker

### Why joining clips drifts

Arabic often takes longer to say than the English it translates. Join the voiced clips end to end and every sentence that runs a little long pushes the next one later. A few minutes in, the narrator is describing a slide that has already gone.

English original

1

2

3

4

Joined end to end

1

2

3

4 late

Placed at each start

1

2

3

4

0:00

0:10

0:20

0:30

0:40

Joined clips drift later with every sentence; placed clips start with the speaker. Clip 3 ran long and was fitted to its slot

### Place every clip on the original timeline

Each transcript segment keeps its original start time. Its Arabic clip is placed at that start, never after the previous clip. When a clip is longer than its slot, a fit ladder shortens or speeds it up until it fits, so the voice stays with the speaker for the whole lecture.

### Learning starts before the dub finishes

The study pack (summary, key terms and their Arabic meanings) is built before anything is translated or voiced. The target is a study pack in about 30 to 40 seconds and a full dub in about 2 to 3 minutes for a 10-minute lecture. Those are spec targets, not measured figures.

### Swappable providers, validated output

Speech-to-text, language models and voice each sit behind an adapter, so the pipeline never imports a vendor SDK. Structured calls ask for JSON and validate it with Pydantic: invalid output gets one retry with the error attached, then the router moves to the next provider.

The hard part of Arabic dubbing isn’t translation. It is time.

Read the full Dubljly case study.

Saad Al-Tamari

Full-stack AI engineer in Amman and co-founder of SKAI Group. I build AI products end to end, from the agents and data underneath to the app people use.

# When not to use your own gateway · Saad Tamari

URL: https://saadaltamari.com/writing-bypass-gateway

Home

/

Writing

/

Build note

## When not to use your own gateway

I built a gateway that every app in the firm goes through. Then I built one platform that deliberately goes around it, and I would defend that call in any review.

Saad Al-Tamari

From the work: Data Sync Platform · Mar–Aug 2026

2 min read

Data pipelines

Architecture

Agents

The Data Sync Platform pulls external systems (CRM, a knowledge base, meeting transcripts) into the shared 87-table schema. It is configured through a chat interface rather than code, and it runs as twelve agents, each with one job.

Fetch

with pagination

Map

fields to columns

Resolve

new · update · duplicate · conflict

Transform

enums and foreign keys

Validate

against live constraints

Write

bulk, with audit trail

Reconcile

counts and anomalies

The seven core agents that run on every sync. Four more handle source-specific content, and one chat agent drives it all

### Plugins are rows, not code

Adding a data source means creating a configuration row, not deploying a code file. The seven core agents handle any REST API given the right config, which is why a new integration can be set up from a chat window in minutes. The chat agent can discover an API, propose mappings, create the configuration, trigger a sync, explain an error and roll back.

### The numbers that made the call

The gateway is built for app traffic: single operations, permissions, rate limits. It has no bulk upsert. Routed through it, one 150-record sync becomes 395+ HTTP round trips, runs straight into the rate limit, and makes the gateway a single point of failure for bulk traffic it was never designed for.

Through the gateway

395+ calls

Direct bulk write

one write

One 150-record sync, two paths

### Going around it without going dark

Bypassing the gateway did not mean bypassing accountability. The platform still writes audit entries and source-mapping rows, so the gateway’s view of the data stays complete. Anyone reading the logs sees the sync exactly as if it had gone through the front door.

### Safety nets for bulk writes

Dry run

The full pipeline runs with the writer switched off and produces a preview report before anything is committed.

Rollback

Every sync is tagged. Inserts are deleted and updates reverted to their prior values from the audit log.

Two ways to make a bulk write reversible

Knowing when not to route through your own abstraction matters more than building the abstraction.

Saad Al-Tamari

Full-stack AI engineer in Amman and co-founder of SKAI Group. I build AI products end to end, from the agents and data underneath to the app people use.

# Why my context engine leaves budget unspent · Saad Tamari

URL: https://saadaltamari.com/writing-context-budget

Home

/

Writing

/

Build note

## Why my context engine leaves budget unspent

Past a point, adding context makes answers worse while cost and latency keep rising. Most retrieval systems have nothing that ever says stop. I built one that does.

Saad Al-Tamari

From the work: Predictive Context Engine · Jun–Aug 2026

2 min read

Context engineering

Agents

LLM cost

The Predictive Context Engine decides what an investment agent should actually see for a given task. It is a compiler, not a search box: every compose runs through nine stages and leaves a record you can audit months later.

Classify

Profile

versioned

Safety gate

Score value

Allocate

budget

Assemble

Band

trust

Probe

Emit

snapshot

The nine stages of one compose, each inspectable in the operator console

### Pack by value per token, then stop

Candidates are ranked by the value they add per token. Packing continues only while the next item clears a marginal-utility threshold. When it doesn’t, allocation stops, even with budget left over.

Illustrative shape, not measured data: the engine stops where the next item adds less than it costs

Allocation

simplified

for item in ranked_by_value_per_token(candidates):

if marginal_utility(item) < threshold:

break # stop, even with budget left

if item.tokens > budget_left:

reject(item, "over budget"); continue

pack(item)

reject_rest(reason="below threshold")

### “Why not” is as auditable as “why”

Every item that was left out is recorded with its reason. When an answer is wrong, the question is usually what the agent didn’t see, and that is now a query rather than a guess.

### Injection is a boundary, not a filter

Untrusted content is scanned and dropped rather than cleaned up, and low-trust sources are structurally barred from the instruction band. That rule is enforced in code and again by a database constraint, so a bug in one layer doesn’t open the door.

Filter approach

Clean up suspicious text, then pass it along with everything else. One missed pattern and it reaches the instructions.

Boundary approach

Low-trust sources can never enter the instruction band. Enforced in code, and again by a database CHECK constraint.

Two ways to handle prompt injection; the engine uses the second

### It never hard-fails

An LLM summary degrades to a deterministic extract, embeddings degrade to lexical similarity, and a timeout returns a valid fallback instead of an error.

### A learning loop that can’t approve itself

Every compose is content-addressed and snapshot-backed, so it replays byte for byte. The engine proposes its own policy changes from measured evidence, and is structurally forbidden from applying them. A person approves, and reverting is one click. Before it trusts its own measurements, it calibrates its LLM judge against human labels.

Leaving budget unspent looks like waste. It is the cheapest quality improvement I know.

Saad Al-Tamari

Full-stack AI engineer in Amman and co-founder of SKAI Group. I build AI products end to end, from the agents and data underneath to the app people use.

# Mission control for 350 agents · Saad Tamari

URL: https://saadaltamari.com/writing-control-plane

Home

/

Writing

/

Build note

## Mission control for 350 agents

Once 350+ agents run across 35+ apps, the first question stops being “is the model good?” It becomes: which agent is failing, what is it costing, and can I stop it without a deploy?

Saad Al-Tamari

From the work: Agent Control Panel · Feb–Aug 2026

3 min read

Agent ops

Observability

LLM cost

The Agent Control Panel was my answer at Decasonic: one login where every agent is observable, measurable and remotely controllable. It runs as a modular monolith, one Node process serving the API and the React app, with 9 tables and about 60 endpoints. No message broker, no worker fleet. The interesting decisions were about who it serves and what it refuses to hide.

### Four people, four questions

Operators

Is anything broken or burning money?

Outages and runaway spend, at a glance

Prompt engineers

Can I change it safely?

Edit, version and roll back without a deploy

Finance

What does each agent cost?

Token and dollar cost per agent, per app, per day

Developers

How do I connect a new app?

A five-step integration wizard

The four audiences the control plane serves, and the question each one asks first

### A health score anyone can read

Every connected app reports heartbeats and runs. Each agent gets a status (running, idle, paused, stopped or error) and a rolling health score recomputed on every run and heartbeat. I kept the formula deliberately simple, so an operator can check it in their head.

health = 100 − (errors in the last 20 runs ÷ 20 × 100)

Example: 3 errors in 20 runs

health 85

The rolling health score, with an example window of 20 runs (orange marks an error)

### Control without redeploying

Pause, resume, stop or restart an agent, swap its model, or push a new system prompt, while the target app keeps running. Commands travel as HMAC-SHA256-signed webhooks with exponential-backoff retry, and each one has a visible lifecycle so nobody wonders whether it landed.

Command

pause · model · prompt

Pending

queued and signed

Sent

webhook delivered

Acknowledged

the app confirms

Failed

retry with backoff

Every remote command moves through the same visible lifecycle

Prompts are versioned assets with one-click rollback. Feedback folds straight into a new version through tags like [INSTRUCTION], [IMPROVEMENT], [BUG FIX] and [KEEP DOING], and an AI reviewer scores answers from 0 to 100 with a written reason.

### The platform watches itself

The panel’s own AI features are modelled as eight real internal agents, so the platform’s LLM spend is tracked with exactly the same machinery as everyone else’s.

Integration Analyzer

Code Generator

Quality Reviewer

Pricing Searcher A

Pricing Searcher B

Pricing Judge

Error Explainer

Error Solver

The eight internal agents, each with its own editable prompt and model

### Prices that check their own sources

Cost tracking is only as good as the price table behind it, and model prices change. So pricing discovery follows a protocol that spends tokens only when it has to.

Public pricing API

free and deterministic

Two searchers

run in parallel, only on failure

Disagree?

each re-checks against the other

Judge

a third model decides

The pricing discovery protocol. Every step goes to a capped audit log, with per-model cooldowns and a global concurrency cap

### Small things that matter in production

- A heartbeat can never silently un-pause an agent someone stopped.

- Token usage is upserted atomically, so concurrent heartbeats can’t lose counts.

- When a provider fails, the fallback chain answers and the UI shows an amber badge, so an operator is never misled about which model replied.

- Prompt and feedback bodies are base64-encoded on the way in, because a production firewall kept reading legitimate prompt text as an attack.

You can’t improve agents you can’t see. Visibility first, then control, then cost.

Saad Al-Tamari

Full-stack AI engineer in Amman and co-founder of SKAI Group. I build AI products end to end, from the agents and data underneath to the app people use.

# Let the code decide, let the model explain · Saad Tamari

URL: https://saadaltamari.com/writing-fair-matching

Home

/

Writing

/

Build note

## Let the code decide, let the model explain

300 founders, VCs and LPs in one room for one day, and every attendee asking the same question: who should I be talking to right now, and what do I say?

Saad Al-Tamari

From the work: Web3 Investor Day app · Apr–Jul 2026

2 min read

Matching

Privacy

Product engineering

I built the whole platform for Decasonic’s Investor Day solo: an Expo mobile app, a React admin console and an Express API, about 60,000 hand-written lines of TypeScript. The part worth writing about is how it decided who should meet whom.

300

attendees, live

21

sessions, 47 speakers

~124

API operations

188

unit tests

The event, and the system behind it

### The model never decides who matches

The pair-scoring function is pure, unit-tested code with no LLM in it. It decides who matches. The model’s only job is to write the human-readable reason, after the decision is made.

Score every pair

pure, tested function

Exclude colleagues

domain normalization

Cap per company

no fund hoards the room

Starvation floor

nobody gets zero

LLM writes the why

explains, never decides

The matching pipeline: deterministic until the very last step

### Fair by construction

Colleagues never match each other. Per-company caps stop one fund from taking every good introduction. A starvation floor guarantees that nobody ends the day with zero introductions, which is the failure a pure “best score wins” system produces for quieter attendees.

### Lunch, as an algorithm

Lunch ran as a rotation: 9 companies, 9 timed rounds, and every attendee routed so they see every company once. A state machine invalidates a live rotation rather than corrupting it if something changes mid-event.

T1

T2

T3

T4

T5

T6

T7

T8

T9

R1

R2

R3

R4

R5

R6

R7

R8

R9

One attendee’s lunch route: a different table (T) in each round (R), every company visited once

### Privacy has to reach the prompt

Some attendees chose to hide their name. Masking it in the API response is not enough: if the full record reaches the model, the generated text can still name them. So masking happens server-side before any surface sees the data, including the LLM prompt.

Masked in the response only

The API hides the name, but the model saw it, and writes “you should meet Sarah from…” in a recommendation.

Masked before every surface

The record is masked on the server first. The app, the admin console and the prompt all receive the same masked data.

Why privacy is enforced as architecture, not as a filter on the way out

### Boring guarantees

- Scanning a QR code twice can’t double-count a check-in: idempotency is enforced by a database constraint, never read-then-write.

- One OpenAPI spec generates the typed client and validation, so the app and the API cannot drift apart.

- Every admin change writes to an audit log.

Use the model for what it is good at, language. Keep the decisions in code you can test.

Saad Al-Tamari

Full-stack AI engineer in Amman and co-founder of SKAI Group. I build AI products end to end, from the agents and data underneath to the app people use.
