# A 200 doesn’t mean your data is useful · Saad Tamari

URL: https://saadaltamari.com/writing-gateway-200

Home

/

Writing

/

Build note

## A 200 doesn’t mean your data is useful

Every write through the gateway came back 200. The dashboards were still empty. So I stopped trusting status codes and audited the data itself.

Saad Al-Tamari

From the work: MCP Hub data audit · 2026

3 min read

Data quality

MCP gateway

Postgres

At Decasonic, 35+ apps and 350+ AI agents write into one shared Postgres schema through a gateway I built. The gateway checks keys, permissions and rate limits, logs every request and translates raw database errors into messages an app can act on. By every operational metric it was healthy.

And yet the views that depended on that data, like an action portal answering “what signals are about this company?”, came back thin or empty. The requests were arriving. The data was not doing its job.

App writes a signal

generated integration code

Gateway

200 OK

Database

row saved, linked to nothing

Where the problem hides: the request succeeds, the data is orphaned

### Success codes measure delivery, not meaning

A 200 tells you the request was accepted. It says nothing about whether the row is linked to anything, whether a junction table was written, or whether the value in a UUID column is a UUID. When most of your write code is generated by AI builders, those are exactly the things that drift.

### Five ways a successful write goes wrong

- Casing against CHECK constraints. About 400 failures, nearly all of them 'prod' sent where the schema expects 'PROD'.

- Plausible but wrong column names. About 30 failures from generated code guessing a name that sounds right.

- Missing junction writes. Zero rows in every junction table, so nothing could answer which signals belong to which company.

- Missing foreign keys. The agent on execution logs was filled on 0 of 1,021 rows. Contacts were linked to a company on 0 of 57.

- Bad types. 'test-123' and '[object Object]' shipped as UUIDs.

Agent set on execution logs

0 / 1,021

Company set on contacts

0 / 57

Signals linked to their run, before

0 / 78

Signals linked to their run, after

777 / 864

Foreign-key fill rates found by the audit. A 200 on every one of these writes

### Fix it once, where it starts

The gateway onboards new apps by generating their integration code from the schema. When the very first integration hit foreign-key violations, the cause was the generator: it wasn’t passing relationship information into the prompt. I fixed it there, once, and every integration after it inherited the fix.

For the apps already live, I wrote a standard four-section fix prompt for each app and closed permission gaps in four of them.

Signals flowing, before

78

Signals flowing, after

864

Agent runs recorded, before

0

Agent runs recorded, after

72

Before and after the fixes, across the nine connected apps. Each pair is on its own scale

### Regressions happen on redeploy

The audit was not a one-time cleanup. One app lost 11 of its 15 table integrations in a single redeploy, and its writes still came back 200. Data health needs checking after every deploy, the same way tests do.

### What I would do from day one

- Measure meaning, not status: foreign-key fill rates, junction row counts, and type validity per app.

- Enforce enums and casing at the gateway, and return an error that names the allowed values.

- Generate clients from a schema contract that carries human-written descriptions, so code knows a status column is a deal stage, not just a string.

- Run the health check after every redeploy, not once a quarter.

A gateway 200 tells you the request arrived. Only the data tells you whether it was worth sending.

Saad Al-Tamari

Full-stack AI engineer in Amman and co-founder of SKAI Group. I build AI products end to end, from the agents and data underneath to the app people use.

# Evaluating RAG end to end without fooling yourself

URL: https://saadaltamari.com/writing-rag-eval

Home

/

Writing

/

Field guide

## Evaluating RAG end to end without fooling yourself

One accuracy number blends six different failures. Here is how to measure each layer, tie it to the end-to-end result, and report intervals that hold up.

Saad Al-Tamari

Field guide · End-to-end RAG evaluation

8 min read

Evaluation

RAG

Statistics

LLM-as-judge

A RAG system can fail in its index, retriever, reranker, packing, generator or citations, and one “answer accuracy” number blends all of them. This note is a method: evaluate each layer, connect the layers to the end-to-end result, and report numbers that would survive a statistician.

### Evaluate the layers, then the system

- Layer | Question it answers | Metric

- Retrieval | Did the evidence come back? | Recall@k at rerank depth, nDCG@10

- Context | Is what we packed useful? | Context precision, distractor rate

- Generation | Is every claim supported? | Claim-level faithfulness

- Correctness | Is the answer right? | Accuracy against a reference, abstention accuracy

- Attribution | Do the citations hold up? | Citation precision and recall

Each row fails differently. An end-to-end score tells you something broke, not where

nDCG rewards ranking highly relevant passages near the top, with a logarithmic discount by position [1]. For RAG, recall at the depth you actually pass to the generator usually predicts answer quality better, because the generator reads everything you pack. Citation precision and recall come from ALCE [2], which builds on the AIS framework for judging whether a statement is attributable to a source [3].

### Your relevance labels are incomplete, and that is a bias

Ground truth is usually built by judging a pool of top results from a few systems. Documents that no pooled system retrieved are never judged and get treated as irrelevant, a bias studied since the TREC era [4]. A new retriever that finds good passages your old one missed is penalised for being better. Before trusting a comparison, judge a sample of the new system’s unjudged results.

Synthetic test sets have their own bias. A question generated from a single chunk tends to reuse that chunk’s wording, which makes lexical retrieval look better than it will on real users, who ask in their own words. Generate from several chunks, paraphrase aggressively, and keep a slice of real queries from logs as the set that decides releases.

### Judge retrieval by what it does to the answer

Relevance labels measure whether a passage is about the question. The generator cares whether the passage helps it answer. eRAG turns that into the metric: feed each retrieved document to the generator on its own, score the output against the reference, and use that score as the document’s label. Salemi and Zamani found this correlates with end-to-end RAG performance better than evaluations built on query-document relevance labels, while using up to 50 times less GPU memory than full end-to-end runs [5].

Retrieve top k

Generate from doc 1 alone

…doc k alone

Score each output

vs reference

Doc labels

aggregate to recall, nDCG

eRAG: label documents by their downstream effect, then compute ordinary ranking metrics on those labels

It also exposes the near-miss problem: a passage can be relevant by any human standard and still lower answer quality [6]. A label that only says “relevant” can’t see that.

### Faithfulness, one claim at a time

“Is this answer grounded?” is too coarse to judge reliably. FActScore splits a long answer into atomic facts and checks each against a knowledge source [7]. RAGChecker applies the idea to RAG: claims from the answer and the reference are checked for entailment against each other and against the retrieved context, which yields diagnostics such as context utilisation, noise sensitivity and hallucination rate rather than one score [8]. RAGAS popularised reference-free versions of these metrics [9].

Generative search: sentences fully supported by citations

51.5%

Generative search: citations that support their sentence

74.5%

CRAG: best LLMs alone

≤ 34%

CRAG: straightforward RAG

44%

CRAG: industry RAG, answered without hallucination

63%

Published baselines: four generative search engines audited by Liu et al., and CRAG’s 4,409 questions

Those are the base rates to beat [10, 11]. CRAG’s headline is worth repeating: adding retrieval in a straightforward way lifted accuracy only from about a third to 44%.

### Validate the judge before you trust it

LLM judges are the only practical way to score claim-level metrics at scale, and their biases are measurable. Zheng et al. documented position, verbosity and self-enhancement bias [12]; Wang et al. showed that swapping the order of two answers can flip a judge’s verdict [13]; Panickssery et al. found judges recognise and favour their own generations [14]. Shankar et al. add a subtler problem, criteria drift: people refine what “good” means while grading, so a rubric fixed in advance quietly stops matching what humans want [15].

Raw agreement

90%. Looks excellent. The judge approves everything, and 90% of answers happen to be good.

Cohen’s kappa

0.00. Agreement corrected for chance: (0.90 − 0.90) / (1 − 0.90). The judge adds nothing.

The same judge, two metrics. Report kappa

So: label 100 to 200 cases by hand, measure agreement with Cohen’s kappa [16], swap positions in every pairwise test, prefer binary claim-level checks over 1 to 10 scales, and re-label a sample whenever the rubric changes.

### Valid intervals from a biased judge

This is the most useful technique in the note. You have a small human-labelled set, say 150 questions, and a large judge-labelled set, say 5,000. The judge is cheap and biased; the humans are unbiased and few. Prediction-powered inference combines them: take the judge’s mean on the large set and correct it by the judge’s average error on the human set [17]. ARES applies it to RAG evaluation [18].

θ̂PP = meanN( judge ) − meann( judge − human )

The correction term removes the judge’s bias. The better the judge agrees with people, the tighter the interval

The estimate stays unbiased even when the judge is systematically optimistic. When the judge agrees with humans most of the time, the interval is far tighter than the 150 human labels could give you alone.

### Do the statistics, including the part people skip

95% interval ≈ p ± 1.96 × √( p (1 − p) / n )

50 questions

± 11.1 pts

100 questions

± 7.8 pts

200 questions

± 5.5 pts

400 questions

± 3.9 pts

1000 questions

± 2.5 pts

Half-widths of the 95% interval at an 80% pass rate, computed exactly. Grey rows can’t resolve a 3 to 5 point change

Miller’s “Adding Error Bars to Evals” lays out the method: report standard errors, use paired differences when two systems answer the same questions, and cluster standard errors when questions are not independent [19]. The last point bites RAG specifically. Eval sets are usually built several questions per document, and questions about the same passage succeed or fail together.

design effect = 1 + (m − 1) ρ → neff = n / design effect

200

questions

10

per document (m)

0.3

intra-document correlation (ρ)

54

effective sample size

Kish’s design effect: 1 + 9 × 0.3 = 3.7, so the honest interval is √3.7 ≈ 1.9× wider than the naive one

That is Kish’s design effect from survey sampling [20]: 200 clustered questions carry about as much information as 54 independent ones. For comparing two systems, count discordant pairs. If 9 questions flipped from fail to pass and 6 from pass to fail, McNemar’s test gives (9 − 6)² / (9 + 6) = 0.6, p ≈ 0.44 [21]: a +3 indistinguishable from chance. The 15 flipped questions are where to read.

### Validate online, not only offline

- Runtime groundedness. Run a cheap claim-support check before an answer ships, and abstain or regenerate when it fails.

- Citation verification. Reject any answer that cites a passage ID that was not in the retrieved set.

- Canaries. Keep a fixed set of questions with known answers and run it on every index rebuild. Re-embedding, chunking changes and deletes break retrieval silently.

- Abstention as a metric. Track correct refusals on unanswerable questions next to accuracy. A system that never says “I don’t know” looks accurate until it isn’t.

- Adversarial slices. Conflicting documents, stale versions, near-miss distractors and planted injections [22], each as its own slice with its own threshold.

A RAG eval is a measurement instrument. Calibrate it against people, put error bars on it, and know which layer every number belongs to.

### References

# RAG past the tutorial: where retrieval quietly breaks

URL: https://saadaltamari.com/writing-rag-retrieval

Home

/

Writing

/

Field guide

## RAG past the tutorial: where retrieval quietly breaks

Chunk, embed, top-k, generate gets you a demo. This is about the second year: the ceilings in that pipeline, the papers that explain them, and what to change.

Saad Al-Tamari

Field guide · Advanced retrieval

12 min read

RAG

Information retrieval

Vector search

Most writing about retrieval-augmented generation stops at the pipeline diagram: chunk, embed, take the top k, generate [1]. This note starts where that one ends. Recall has plateaued, the reranker no longer moves the numbers, and the remaining failures are subtle. Each section is a ceiling in the standard setup, the research that explains it, and what I would change.

### A single vector has a capacity limit

Dense retrieval compresses a passage into one vector and scores it against the query with a dot product [2]. It is fast and it generalises, and it has a geometric ceiling. Weller et al. show that the number of distinct top-k result sets a d-dimensional embedding can return is bounded by d, and the bound holds even when embeddings are optimised directly on the test set [3]. Their LIMIT dataset uses deliberately simple queries and still defeats state-of-the-art embedding models.

In production this shows up on combinatorial queries: “contracts with a termination clause and a foreign counterparty”, “papers that cite A but not B”. The relevant set is an intersection, and one vector per document cannot represent every intersection a user might ask for. More training data does not lift a dimensional bound.

Single vector

One embedding per passage, score = q · d. Every top-k set a user could want has to fit in d dimensions.

Late interaction

One embedding per token, score = Σi maxj qi · dj. Each query term finds its own best match, so conjunctions survive.

Single-vector scoring against ColBERT-style MaxSim scoring

The alternatives each cost something. Late-interaction models such as ColBERT keep a vector per token and score with MaxSim [4]; ColBERTv2’s residual compression is what makes that index affordable [5]. Learned sparse models such as SPLADE expand documents into weighted vocabulary terms and keep the exactness of an inverted index [6]. Cross-encoders read query and passage together and have no capacity bottleneck at all, which is exactly why they belong at the end of the cascade, on a short list [7].

### Hybrid search is coverage, and RRF is mostly a vote

BEIR evaluated retrievers zero-shot across 18 datasets. BM25 held up as a strong baseline out of domain, dense retrievers trained on one domain often underperformed elsewhere, and reranking and late-interaction models were best on average at a much higher cost [8]. Keyword plus vector search is not a hedge. It is two different failure surfaces covering each other.

Reciprocal Rank Fusion is the usual way to merge them [9]. Its constant k changes the behaviour more than most people expect.

RRF(d) = Σlists 1 / (k + rank(d))

- k | Weight at rank 1 | Weight at rank 10 | Rank 1 ÷ rank 10

- 0 | 1.0000 | 0.1000 | 10.00×

- 10 | 0.0909 | 0.0500 | 1.82×

- 60 | 0.0164 | 0.0143 | 1.15×

Computed exactly. At the standard k = 60, one list barely distinguishes its 1st result from its 10th

At k = 60, a document a list ranks 1st gets only 1.15 times the weight of one it ranks 10th. RRF behaves like a vote counter: appearing in both lists matters far more than where you appear in either.

- Doc | BM25 rank | Vector rank | Sum | RRF score | Fused

- Doc B | 3 | 1 | 1/63 + 1/61 | 0.0323 | 1

- Doc A | 1 | 4 | 1/61 + 1/64 | 0.0320 | 2

- Doc E | 4 | 3 | 1/64 + 1/63 | 0.0315 | 3

- Doc C | 2 | – | 1/62 | 0.0161 | 4 (tie)

- Doc D | – | 2 | 1/62 | 0.0161 | 4 (tie)

A worked example at k = 60. Doc E is never first in either list, but both lists agree on it, so it beats Doc C, which only one list liked

That is what you want when the two lists are complementary, and the wrong behaviour when one retriever is clearly better for a query class. For identifier-shaped queries (error codes, SKUs, function names) you want BM25’s first hit to dominate. Lower k for that class, or route those queries to the lexical leg before fusion. And fuse at the depth you rerank: a document missing from a list contributes zero, so fusing two lists of depth 10 silently drops everything one retriever ranked 11th.

### Chunking is a modelling decision

Chunk boundaries decide what can be retrieved together. There are four serious answers, and they fit different question shapes.

- Question shape | What breaks with plain chunks | Index structure that fits

- A fact inside a long section | The answer is split across a boundary | Small-to-big: retrieve sentences, return the parent section

- Pronouns and implied entities | “Revenue rose 12%” with no company named | Contextual chunk headers, or late chunking

- Synthesis across one document | No single chunk contains the answer | A recursive summary tree

- Themes across the corpus | “What are the main risks across all reports?” | Graph community summaries

Pick the index structure from the questions you actually get, not from a default chunk size

Contextual retrieval prepends a short, model-written description of where each chunk sits in its document before embedding and indexing it. Anthropic reported it roughly halved failed retrievals in their tests, with a further gain when combined with reranking [10]. Late chunking reaches a similar goal without an LLM call per chunk: embed the whole document with a long-context encoder, then pool the token embeddings per chunk, so every chunk vector is conditioned on the full document [11]. RAPTOR clusters and recursively summarises chunks into a tree, so a question can match a summary node when no leaf holds the answer [12]. GraphRAG extracts an entity graph, summarises its communities, and answers global questions by map-reducing over those summaries [13]. It is the right tool for “what are the themes” questions, and an expensive one: every chunk passes through an extraction call at indexing time.

### The reranker cannot fix what the first stage never fetched

A cascade is bounded by first-stage recall at the depth you rerank. If the gold passage sits at position 140 and you rerank the top 100, the best cross-encoder available returns a confident wrong answer. The number to watch is first-stage recall@100, not final recall@5.

Index

every chunk

Hybrid first stage

~100 candidates

Cross-encoder or LLM rerank

top ~20

Packed into the prompt

5 to 8

Typical shape of the cascade, not a benchmark. Everything downstream is bounded by the second row

LLM rerankers are now competitive with trained cross-encoders; RankGPT showed listwise reranking with a sliding window over the candidates [14]. Two details matter in production. Listwise rerankers are sensitive to the order candidates arrive in, and aggregating over several shuffled orders measurably improves them [15], which is worth the cost on high-stakes queries. And reranker scores are not calibrated across queries: 0.7 means something different for a short factoid than for a long analytical question. A single global “abstain below 0.5” threshold will be wrong for some query class. Calibrate thresholds per query type, or use the margin between the first and second candidate as the confidence signal.

### The dangerous passage is the near miss

Long context windows do not remove the ordering problem. Liu et al. found models use information at the start and end of the input more reliably than in the middle [16], and Shi et al. showed irrelevant context measurably distracts models even on simple problems [17]. Cuconasu et al. then found something more uncomfortable: passages that rank highly but do not contain the answer hurt accuracy, while adding random documents raised accuracy by up to 35% in their setup [18].

Illustrative shape of the lost-in-the-middle finding, not data from a specific model

Gold

Contains the answer

The only passage you actually want.

Random

Unrelated to the query

Mostly harmless, and in some setups it helped.

Near miss

Looks relevant, no answer

The most damaging. The model treats it as evidence.

Three kinds of passage in a packed context, ordered by how much they hurt

The practical reading is that your worst passages are your reranker’s confident false positives, because they look exactly like evidence. Track a distractor rate on the eval set: the share of packed passages that score as relevant but do not support the answer. Then pack fewer passages, put the strongest first, and restate the question at the end of the prompt.

### Decide whether to retrieve, then check what came back

Not every query needs retrieval, and not every retrieval should be trusted. Self-RAG trains a model to emit reflection tokens that decide when to retrieve and whether the retrieved passages support the output [19]. Corrective RAG adds a lightweight evaluator that grades retrieved documents and triggers a fallback, such as web search or refinement, when confidence is low [20]. You don’t need their training recipes to use the idea: a cheap router in front of retrieval and a sufficiency check after it catch a large class of failures before generation.

On the query side, HyDE embeds a generated hypothetical answer instead of the question [21], and Ma et al. trained a small rewriter with reinforcement learning against downstream answer quality [22]. The trick I’d add: rewriters paraphrase away exact tokens. Send the original query to the lexical leg and the rewritten one to the dense leg, then fuse. You keep the identifier match and gain the semantic expansion.

User query

kept verbatim

BM25 leg

original wording

Rewriter

expand, decompose

Dense leg

rewritten query

Fuse + rerank

at depth 100

Split the query by leg so rewriting never costs you an exact match

### The index is an approximation too

HNSW, the default graph index in most vector databases, is approximate by design [23]. Its recall against exact search is below 1 and moves with parameters like ef_search, and few teams measure it. Sample a few hundred real queries, run brute-force search on them, and compare. If ANN recall@10 is 0.92, no amount of embedding or reranker tuning recovers the missing 8%.

Filters make this worse. Under a restrictive metadata filter, say one tenant and one month, post-filtering an HNSW result can leave almost nothing, and pre-filtering can cut the graph into pieces so the search stalls in a region with no valid nodes. Predicate-aware indexes such as ACORN were built for this case [24]. If you can’t change the index, partition by the most selective filter, which is usually the tenant.

Compression has the same shape. Product quantisation [25] and Matryoshka embeddings, which can be truncated to fewer dimensions [26], cut memory dramatically at some recall cost. The standard recovery is two passes: search with compressed vectors, then rescore the top few hundred with full-precision ones before reranking.

### Your corpus is an attack surface

Anything retrievable can be injected. Greshake et al. demonstrated indirect prompt injection through retrieved content in real LLM-integrated applications [27]. PoisonedRAG measured how little it takes: five malicious texts per target question, in a knowledge base of millions of texts, reached a 90% attack success rate [28].

- Keep provenance on every chunk (source, owner, ingestion time, trust tier) and filter on it at retrieval time.

- Present passages as quoted data, never as instructions, and never let retrieved text change which tools the model may call.

- Watch for new documents that suddenly rank first for many unrelated queries. An optimised poison looks exactly like that.

### The checklist I actually use

- Measure first-stage recall at rerank depth, ANN recall against brute force, and distractor rate, as three separate numbers.

- Route identifier-shaped queries to lexical search, and tune RRF’s k per query class.

- Choose the chunking strategy from question shape, not from a default size.

- Calibrate abstention thresholds per query type.

- Version the embedding model together with the index, and migrate through a shadow index rather than in place.

- Keep provenance on every chunk, and filter on it.

Every ceiling in RAG is a retrieval ceiling first. The model can only reason over what you hand it.

# 28 apps, 756 connections: why the database is the contract

URL: https://saadaltamari.com/writing-schema-contract

Home

/

Writing

/

Build note

## 28 apps, 756 connections: why the database is the contract

Decasonic had 300+ agents spread across 10 to 15 products, each with its own database and no shared memory. I replaced the mesh with one rule: every app writes what it knows to one schema and reads what it needs from it.

Saad Al-Tamari

From the work: DDS v3 schema · Jan–Aug 2026

2 min read

Data architecture

Postgres

Multi-agent

No app calls another app’s API for data. The database is the contract. It sounds conservative. It is the reason the platform grew from about 10 products to 35+ without integration work eating the project.

### The arithmetic of a mesh

If every app can talk to every other app, the number of possible connections grows as n × (n − 1). With one shared contract it grows as n. The gap is small at five apps and absurd at thirty.

Mesh: n × (n − 1)

Shared database: n

x-axis: number of apps

Exact counts, not estimates: at 28 apps a mesh needs 756 connections; a shared schema needs 28

### What 87 tables are made of

DDS v3 shipped as one 1,571-line SQL migration: 87 tables and 73 enum types.

Primary entities

35

Junction tables

41

Sync tables

6

Gateway tables

5

The 87 tables by kind. Junction tables outnumber entities on purpose: relationships are first-class

### Decisions, written down and locked

Nine structural decisions were recorded before the first table was created, so nobody had to rediscover them under pressure. Among them:

UUID primary keys

Junction tables over JSONB arrays

Identity-centric ownership

Audit log on every change

CHECK constraints over Postgres enums

Soft deletes

Environment separation

Optimistic concurrency

Some of the nine locked structural decisions

### A schema that describes itself

A schema-discovery call returns every table with its columns, types, foreign keys, constraints and human-written descriptions as JSON. Every downstream app and every AI code generator reads that one document, so generated integration code never guesses a column name.

Schema + descriptions

written by people

Discovery JSON

one call, always current

Code generator

reads meaning, not just shape

Integration client

real column names

From schema to working client, without anyone copying column names by hand

### When sources disagree

A CRM, a meeting transcript and an agent can all claim a different value for the same field. A system-of-record priority model resolves those conflicts deterministically, field by field, so the answer doesn’t depend on which write arrived last.

A shared schema is slower to design and faster to live with. That trade is almost always worth it.

Saad Al-Tamari

# Skills that get better by losing · Saad Tamari

URL: https://saadaltamari.com/writing-skills-loop

Home

/

Writing

/

Build note

## Skills that get better by losing

A skill is a block of instructions an agent loads at runtime. Most teams write them once and hope. We tested them against real agents, and let the losers be rewritten.

Saad Al-Tamari

From the work: Agent Skills OS · May–Aug 2026

2 min read

Agent skills

Evaluation

Prompting

Agent Skills OS is a content system and test lab for agent instructions. A skill is written, versioned, A/B tested against a real agent, judged, improved if it loses, and only then deployed into production prompts.

Write

or generate a skill

Version

immutable snapshot

Test twice

real agent, with and without

Judge

structured verdict

Rewrite

only if it lost

Assign

pin a version per agent

The closed loop. A rewritten skill goes back into testing as a new version

### Test on the real thing

The test lab runs the same prompt through a real, synced production agent twice: once with its normal system prompt, once with the skill added, using that agent’s actual model. An LLM judge compares the two outputs and returns a structured verdict. Results reflect how the agent really behaves, not a simulation of it.

### Losing is useful

If the skill loses, a frontier model rewrites it into a new version, using both test outputs and the judge’s reasoning. That version is tested again. Skills improve through evaluation rather than through whoever last edited them.

### Fail open, on purpose

Agents pull their enabled skills at prompt-fetch time. If this service is unreachable, agents fall back to their base prompts instead of breaking. It is a deliberate availability trade: an outage in the skills service must never take down the agent fleet.

Fail closed

Skills service down, so every agent that depends on it errors. One service takes down the fleet.

Fail open

Skills service down, so agents run on their base prompts. Quality dips a little; nothing breaks.

The availability trade the service is built around

### Suggestions you can trust

A suggestions engine reads the real skills, agents, tests and assignments and proposes new skills. Any agent or skill identifier it hallucinates is filtered out by schema validation before it reaches the screen.

If you can’t measure a skill against the agent that will use it, you are guessing.
